candidate.label: Idealism and conscious illusion
candidate.motion: Does analytic idealism adequately explain consciousness?
candidate.sourceNote: Public English captions cover the complete substantive conversation published by Curt Jaimungal in 2023. Selected speaker transitions and uncertain passages were checked against the recording. The duplicated opening preview, promotional material and moderator logistics receive no separate credit; no later substantive discussion is omitted. One unidentified, nonmaterial repeated boundary question is excluded from quotation and credit. Short quotations retain verified source wording; argument cards are faithful condensations. Blackmore rejects materialism and offers a limited critical method, not a completed rival metaphysics.

strengths: Unifies experience, perception, neural correlation, and private perspectives within one category while directly confronting the hard problem's transition.
Uses dashboard and dissociation models to connect idealism with familiar cognition and measurable clinical observations.
Accepts brute regularities and a fictional personal self, creating substantial common ground with Blackmore's concerns.

blunders.text: Treats field descriptions as nearly settling contested metaphysics and generalizes a bounded-particle criticism beyond Blackmore's alternatives.
Answers revisability with caricature and historical speculation instead of a condition that could count against idealism.

strengths: Limits her burden to critical diagnosis, rejects materialism, and avoids pretending to possess a complete rival metaphysics.
Targets explanatory gain, ontology-neutral perception, neural mapping, and extrapolation from clinical to cosmic dissociation.
Shows calibration by conceding brute regularities, welcoming controlled evidence, and limiting claims about research not recently reviewed.

blunders.text: Leaves her opening method broad until later clarification, giving Kastrup legitimate grounds to request a definite target.
Sometimes invokes materialist explanation despite rejecting materialism, obscuring whether her challenge concerns science or ontology.

finalArgument.thesis: Analytic idealism is comparatively adequate when experience is basic and bodies, perception, and private perspectives are structured appearances within one field.
premises: All descriptions of nature occur within experience, so quantitative descriptions cannot eliminate the qualitative reality through which they are known.
An experiential ontology avoids the additional transition required when nonexperiential matter is asked to generate qualitative awareness.
Evolutionary perception can compress salient information without requiring appearances to resemble the external experiential processes they track.
Biological regulation can mark inferentially isolated perspectives, with neural activity expressing rather than manufacturing corresponding inner states.
Lawful behavior concerns properties of whatever exists and therefore does not independently require a nonmental ontological category.
finalArgument.conclusion: Together these claims form a unified proposal whose success depends on deriving constrained boundaries and appearance mappings that rivals cannot equally explain.

newArguments.text: Idealism can predict structural correspondences between phenomenal and neural organization without claiming production. It should specify which experiential transformations preserve, divide, or recombine observable patterns across anesthesia, attention, and dissociation. Mappings fixed before observation and differing from production accounts would turn intrinsic-extrinsic identity from retrospective reinterpretation into a comparative empirical program.

newArguments.title: Boundary Gradient Argument
newArguments.text: Biological systems exhibit graded informational closure through metabolism, membranes, prediction, and selective communication. Idealism could link these degrees to graded privacy and address colonies, symbioses, and temporary integration without stipulating sharp subjects. This would connect ordinary access limits with clinical dissociation while avoiding the claim that every informational separation creates an experiencer.

newArguments.title: Economy Beyond Counting
newArguments.text: Ontological economy concerns explanatory commitments, not category count. Idealism should show that experiential dynamics explain perception, causation, and individuation with fewer bridging laws than rivals. The comparison must count principles connecting universal mentality to personal minds. Independently motivated constraints make economy substantive, whereas renaming unexplained correlations leaves one-category simplicity superficial.

finalArgument.thesis: Analytic idealism remains underdetermined because its strongest descriptions fit rival ontologies while its dissociation mechanism exceeds the evidence presented.
premises: Fitness-shaped dashboards explain appearance without deciding whether underlying reality is mental, physical, neutral, or processual.
Clinical dissociation demonstrates partitioned access within organisms but not partitions within universal subjectivity.
Calling neural activity mentality's outward appearance redescribes correlation unless the theory specifies why particular experiences map to particular patterns.
Physical field models replace bounded particles, yet mathematical nonlocality does not entail one experiencing subject.
A critic can test explanatory adequacy without supplying a complete rival ontology or denying phenomenal experience.
finalArgument.conclusion: Idealism therefore owes discriminating mechanisms and predictions, not merely compatibility and category reduction, before becoming adequate relative to alternatives.

newArguments.title: Multiple Realizability Challenge
newArguments.text: If biology identifies dissociative boundaries, the theory must explain why different biological organizations yield subjects and whether nonbiological systems qualify. Similar isolation occurs in nervous systems, colonies, immune networks, and artificial architectures. Without a rule, biology becomes a label rather than an explanation, while rivals can accept the cited correlations without treating metabolism as dissociation's appearance.

newArguments.title: Mapping Specificity Objection
newArguments.text: The two-view proposal must explain why one circuit alters color while another alters memory, and why mappings remain stable across observers. Physicalist, neutral-monist, and dual-aspect theories also expect correlation. Idealism therefore needs independently motivated transformation rules constraining which observable organizations correspond to which qualitative structures.

newArguments.title: Asymmetric Revisability Test
newArguments.text: A worldview gains credibility by stating what counts against it. Here idealism accommodates regularity, neural correlation, anomalous experience, and absent laboratory telepathy, risking equal compatibility with contrary outcomes. Blackmore's controlled-evidence standard suggests defining observations that lower confidence in porosity or one-field subjectivity. Until failure conditions are explicit, accommodation is not confirmation.
